questions.question: Router A learned the 10.0.0.0/8 route from neighbor B over their shared link. When A later sends updates to B, it omits that prefix entirely. Which loop-prevention rule explains the omission?
questions.explanation: Advertising a route back toward the neighbor it was learned from could let that neighbor route the destination through A, forming a loop; split horizon forbids sending a route out the interface it arrived on, which is exactly the omission described.

questions.question: After a topology change, EIGRP runs a finite-state computation that diffuses queries and replies among neighbors to guarantee a loop-free path - the same machinery that pre-qualifies backup feasible successors. Which algorithm does it use?
questions.explanation: EIGRP's loop-free route computation - including the reported-distance checks that validate feasible successors - is performed by DUAL, the Diffusing Update Algorithm.

questions.question: Two newly connected OSPF routers multicast small packets to 224.0.0.5 to discover each other and verify matching parameters before forming an adjacency. Which OSPF packet type are they exchanging?
questions.explanation: Neighbor discovery on the AllSPFRouters multicast address and the exchange of timers/flags that must match before adjacency are done by OSPF Type 1 Hello packets; DBD, LSR, LSU, and LSAck come afterward.

questions.question: After a link failure, LSAs flood through the area and within seconds every router's table agrees on the new topology again. What is this restored, mutually consistent state called?
questions.explanation: The period during which all routers relearn and agree on identical routing information after a change is convergence; a network in that steady state is said to be converged.

questions.question: A BGP router receives a prefix carrying a path attribute that lists '65001 65002 65003'; it will reject the route if its own AS number already appears in that list, preventing loops. Which attribute is this?
questions.explanation: AS_PATH records every autonomous system a route has traversed; seeing its own AS in the list means the route already looped through and must be dropped - and its length also feeds best-path selection.

questions.question: EIGRP's best path to a prefix has metric 1000 and a feasible alternate has metric 1800. The admin configures a multiplier of 2 so traffic is shared across both unequal paths proportionally. Which feature is this?
questions.explanation: Multiplying the successor metric by the variance value (1000 x 2 = 2000) admits any feasible successor with metric <= 2000 into the forwarding table, enabling unequal-cost load sharing - unique to EIGRP.

questions.question: All OSPF routers inside an area must hold identical, synchronized copies of every flooded LSA. In which structure are those copies stored?
questions.explanation: Flooded LSAs are collected into each router's link-state database, and identical LSDBs within an area are what let every router run SPF and agree on the same shortest paths.

questions.question: A router learns 10.4.0.0/16 from both RIP and OSPF, and the OSPF route is installed because its protocol is trusted at a lower administrative distance. What is OSPF's administrative distance?
questions.explanation: Cisco's default distances rank OSPF at 110 - more trusted than RIP's 120 but less than EIGRP's 90 - so the OSPF-learned copy of the prefix wins the table.

questions.question: A rogue router injected bogus LSAs into an OSPF domain; neighbors now require a keyed MD5 digest on every routing packet before accepting it. Which protection was enabled?
questions.explanation: Requiring a shared keyed digest on routing updates proves they come from a legitimate peer, rejecting injected LSAs - that is route (routing-protocol/neighbor) authentication.

questions.question: An ISP router peers with a customer's router in a different autonomous system; the session runs with TTL 1 across the AS boundary and learned routes may be readvertised to other peers. Which BGP session type is this?
questions.explanation: Peering between different AS numbers is external BGP (eBGP); sessions are normally single-hop (TTL 1), and eBGP-learned routes can be advertised onward, unlike iBGP's full-mesh restriction.

questions.question: A route redistributed into EIGRP from another domain is installed only when nothing better exists, because the router distrusts it at a higher administrative distance than internal EIGRP's 90. What is that distance?
questions.explanation: Internal EIGRP routes carry AD 90 while external (redistributed) EIGRP routes are demoted to 170, so they lose to almost any more-preferred source of the same prefix.

questions.question: Two routers inside AS 65000 peer in a full mesh, and routes learned from one internal peer are never readvertised to other internal peers. Which BGP session type is this?
questions.explanation: Peering within one autonomous system is iBGP; its loop-prevention rule forbids passing iBGP-learned routes to other iBGP peers, which is exactly why the full mesh (or a route reflector) is required.

questions.question: Router R3 has physical interfaces 10.0.0.1 and 192.168.1.1 plus loopbacks 1.1.1.1 and 2.2.2.2, and no manually configured router ID. Applying OSPF's selection order, which configured address becomes the router ID?
alternatives: the higher of the two loopbacks
questions.explanation: Without a manual ID, OSPF first prefers loopbacks over physical interfaces, then picks the numerically highest: between 1.1.1.1 and 2.2.2.2 the winner is the 2.2.2.2 loopback - not the higher physical 192.168.1.1.

questions.question: Routers in area 1 see routes to subnets that live in area 2; the ABR generated summary advertisements describing those networks to the other area. Which LSA type carried them?
questions.explanation: Router LSAs (Type 1) describe links inside an area and network LSAs (Type 2) describe transit networks, but only ABR-originated Type 3 Summary LSAs carry prefixes between areas.

questions.question: Two exit routers reach the same prefix and every well-known BGP attribute ties, until a Cisco-proprietary value - locally significant and never advertised beyond the router - picks the winner. Which attribute decides first?
questions.explanation: Cisco's Weight is checked first in best-path selection (higher wins) and is local to the router, so it precedes LOCAL_PREF, AS_PATH, MED, and the rest of the tiebreakers.

questions.question: A RIP router advertises a network with a hop count of 16. What does this hop count signify?
questions.explanation: RIP treats 16 hops as infinity; any network at 16 hops is considered unreachable, enforcing the 15-hop maximum.

questions.question: A router learns 192.168.40.0/24 from both OSPF (administrative distance 110) and EIGRP (administrative distance 90). Which route is installed in the routing table?
alternatives: the route with the lower administrative distance
questions.explanation: When multiple protocols offer the same prefix, the router prefers the lowest administrative distance: EIGRP's 90 beats OSPF's 110.

questions.question: OSPF calculates cost as reference bandwidth divided by interface bandwidth. With the default 100 Mbps reference, what is the OSPF cost of a 5 Mbps interface?
questions.explanation: Cost = 100 Mbps / 5 Mbps = 20.

questions.question: An EIGRP backup path sits in the topology table because its reported distance is below the successor's feasible distance, so it can be promoted instantly without running DUAL again. What is this standby route called?
questions.explanation: A loop-free backup that satisfies the feasibility condition (reported distance < current feasible distance) is stored as a feasible successor and promoted the moment the successor fails, with no recomputation.

questions.question: A floating static route with administrative distance 200 is configured for a prefix also learned via OSPF. Under what condition does the static route take over?
questions.answer: when the OSPF-learned route fails or is removed
alternatives: only when the primary route disappears
when the better route is lost
questions.explanation: A floating static route's higher AD keeps it out of the table until the dynamically learned route (lower AD) becomes unavailable.
